title: Chapter Thirty-Five: Yu
bio: “Yu” — An ancient legend tells of a creature in the water that holds sand in its mouth and spits it at people’s shadows; those it strikes never know where the blow came from, they only feel the pain. As the saying goes: the one struck through his shadow never sees the shape of what struck him.
paragraphs: Deep winter in Xi’an: dry and cold outside, but the heating in the office was running full blast. Old Zheng’s desk, as ever, was piled with documents and hardware modules, spread across it in a mess.

By the window, Zhang Hailu and Old Zheng sat on the sofas by the coffee table talking business — Hailu in the single armchair at the side, Old Zheng on the three-seater, a thick stack of technical materials spread on the coffee table between them. Old Zheng lit a cigarette, took two drags and flicked the ash into the ashtray.

Zhang Hailu turned another page of the report he was holding and said, “It’s the end of the year, and the Sixth Academy’s phase-two money has finally come in. Eighty percent has arrived in total now, sixteen million. There’s twenty percent left — the final acceptance payment, as they put it — to be settled in the first quarter of next year.”
Old Zheng said, “First quarter next year? If they don’t drag it into the second half, we’ll be lucky. How much did Wang Renhou settle this year?”

Zhang Hailu said, “His orders for the whole year topped three million units. At sixty fen a unit in cost-down commission, that’s 1.8 million, not a day late — it came through at the end of last month. I asked him for the customs declarations, and the numbers match up.”

Old Zheng took a drag and said, “Guangdong bosses really do keep their word. It’s so different from the way private companies up north do things. No wonder companies in Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Guangdong get big, right?”

Hailu said, “Wang Renhou’s really made a killing these past few years. Those markets he sells into are so obscure, and the product’s technical bar isn’t high, yet he’s managed volumes this big. Who’d have thought?”
Old Zheng: “That’s just his good fortune. Still, we got a bit of the soup too.”

Zhang Hailu said, “Isn’t that the truth — when things were hardest, his bit of cash was what kept us going. But with this Sixth Academy payment settled, we’ve finally pulled through. Salaries, suppliers, everything we owed — it’s all cleared, right? How much profit will we have for the year?”
Old Zheng said, “A few million. I’ll work out the detailed accounts in the next few days.”

Zhang Hailu said, “Mr. Zheng, I remember you telling me back then that Wu You had promised that once we made money on this project, he’d make the technical profit shares for our team official. I remember you said you have ten percent. I looked the other day and your business registration hasn’t been changed yet, has it?”

Old Zheng glanced at him and nodded. He stubbed out his cigarette and said, “Right. The agreement’s signed, but the shareholders’ round of signatures never got finished, and then we got busy…” Old Zheng remembered again how he’d asked Wu You back then about the three million transferred out to buy the old shares. Those six percent had ended up in a partnership entity in Shanghai, and they too had been promised to him back then. Old Zheng thought that since this year’s results had been delivered, it was time to go report to Mr. Wu and get him to make these technical profit shares official. So he said, “Hailu, I’ve been keeping these things in mind too. This time, when I go to Shanghai for the year-end review, I’ll ask Mr. Wu You when the change will be made.”
Zhang Hailu said, “Don’t let this one drag on. And see what’s happening with everyone’s year-end bonuses, too.”

Old Zheng was silent for a moment, then said, “I know. I’ll go to Shanghai next week. Before I go, you get the accounts on this project straight. For the Sixth Academy project — how much cost went in, how much came back, what the gross margin is — list it all out item by item. With the accounts in hand, I’ll have something solid to stand on when I talk to him.”

Hailu said, “Fine. I’ve got the project’s procurement costs and so on, and I can work out the gross margin. Zhu Yiwen’s portion of the procurement costs and the company’s staff costs — I don’t have those.”

Old Zheng said, “I’ve got that part.” He thought to himself: the hidden expenses, too, were on his books alone; that part would have to be submitted to Wu You separately. Then he said, “Tell Cong Shasha to come with me to Shanghai next week for the review.”
Shanghai, Lujiazui.

Outside the huge floor-to-ceiling windows of Wu You’s office, the Huangpu River was gray and murky; through the gaps between the towers you could see the bridges over the Huangpu far off. Wu You sat behind his desk in a dark gray turtleneck, a Starbucks coffee on the desk. When he saw Old Zheng come in he stood, came around the desk to meet him and held out his hand. “Mr. Zheng, Ms. Cong, you’ve made it. Sit.”

On the inner side of Wu You’s office was his desk, with three huge monitors on it side by side. On the other side was a big conference table, and at its far end a mobile TV stand holding a seventy-five-inch Xiaomi TV. On the other side, the glass wall had been covered in white to make one huge whiteboard, with a mind map scrawled across it.
Zheng Zhiyong and Shasha sat together on one side of the conference table, and Wu You pushed the TV over.

Shasha used a PPT to present the overall picture of the Sixth Academy project and a few small private-sector projects, page by page. When she’d finished, Old Zheng looked at Wu You’s expression. Wu You had listened to Shasha’s briefing on the execution of the whole project without showing a thing. The financial figures in the briefing covered revenue and the company’s procurement costs — and those reflected only the 6.7 million Zhang Hailu’s side had spent on procurement. Then Wu You said, “Beautiful work by the team. Thank you all for your hard work. Ms. Cong, you’ve done a great service on the Sixth Academy project — excellent!”
Shasha blushed and said with a smile, “Thank you, Mr. Wu. It was the whole team’s contribution.”

Old Zheng said, “It really was her. Not just that last kick at the goal to win the project and nail down the contract — Ms. Cong’s coordination with the Sixth Academy throughout was excellent, and getting the payment in before year’s end was Ms. Cong’s doing too.” Hearing this, Shasha shot Old Zheng a pleased, smiling look. Old Zheng glanced back at Shasha and said, “Ms. Cong, I’ll report the next part to Mr. Wu on my own. You go on back.”
So Shasha sensibly took her leave of Wu You’s office, thinking she’d wait for Old Zheng at the coffee shop downstairs so they could leave together when he was done.
Old Zheng watched the door of Wu You’s office close behind her, then said, “Mr. Wu, let me give you a separate report, so we can look at this year’s overall financial picture.”

Wu You nodded for Old Zheng to go on, and Old Zheng continued, “Right now our main sales receipts total sixteen million — that’s the Sixth Academy’s money — with four million more in receivables. We also took in a sales commission on a private-sector motor redesign, 1.8 million in total. So total revenue over this period is 21.8 million, booked as of November. The company’s operating costs are currently 360,000 a month; in practice they only started being incurred, and going up, from April. Total accumulated staff costs are about 2.3 million. Hailu’s side’s total procurement cost is 6.7 million, with another 970,000 in procurement payables to be paid after the final payment next year. What we’ve paid the outside collaborator so far is four million, with another four million payable. And then there’s 310,000 in hidden expenses, which I reported to you before. When the company was handed over to me there were five-odd million, and right now we’ve got over ten million in cash on the books.”

Wu You tilted his head and said, “Mr. Zheng, come sit over here with me.” He led Zheng Zhiyong to a chair across from his desk, turned a laptop screen around to face Old Zheng, and showed him a financial statement he had there.

Wu You said, “Mr. Zheng, your accounts and mine don’t seem to quite match. On staff costs, my annual total is 4.22 million — have a look. You’ve got operating costs at 360,000 a month, but in practice the company has to pay the employees’ social insurance and housing fund, and for a few colleagues we have to work with payroll-outsourcing companies outside Xi’an, which costs extra. All in, costs go up about forty percent. On my side it’s 480,000 a month right now. When you first came in, you laid off all the old staff, and the layoffs cost 520,000. The two full-time finance and accounting people I assigned to your project team — their salaries and costs since you took over come to 320,000 in total. So total staff costs aren’t 2.3 million; the statement finance gave me says 4.22 million, with the details in this report. As I recall, finance sends you this figure every month and copies me — this is the annual summary. Also, the whole office building is rented by the company from one of our shareholders, at 1.8 million a year. The company car and your full-time assistant come to 200,000 for the year. Plus the 310,000 in hidden expenses — those are real company outgoings too. Plus everyone flying back and forth, team dinners, the everyday operating costs — since you arrived, that’s over 700,000 all told. Plus the two procurement costs, 14.7 million combined. Add it all up and it seems we’ve spent more than 22 million — more than our total revenue.”

Old Zheng said nothing. Wu You looked at him calmly, thinking to himself: “I did give this Zheng Zhiyong full authority and trust, but life as a boss really isn’t easy. This year I’ve lost tens of millions of my own money in the secondary market again. I’d hoped this company might earn a bit, and in the end it’s another year of running around for nothing.”

What Old Zheng was thinking was: “The car, the assistant, the office — I wasn’t the one who decided we needed any of that. Especially Wu Peng — that’s your nephew, sent over to keep an eye on my work. If it were my own startup, a few of us brothers could have rented a flat and done it.” But after a moment’s thought he remembered again how, when the qualifications had nearly failed, this imposing little building had helped them make their case with the leaders — at the very least it showed that while the team was newly put together, the company had the financial strength. And afterward, plenty of leaders from every department had come here to visit, and the private dining room on the building’s third floor had entertained plenty of local leaders and guests. In this business, maybe a good front really was indispensable sometimes. With that thought Old Zheng said, “Mr. Wu, I understand the state of the accounts on your side. I’m still a technical guy — I’ve never done the books for the whole picture before. With all the mouths to feed this year, men and horses alike, the outgoings really were too big.”
Wu You said, “So what’s the plan for the new year? Whatever happens, we’ve got to make this a company that makes money.”

Old Zheng said, “On this project, what we were fighting for was the Sixth Academy’s name. With the project done, not only has the Sixth Academy recognized us, we’ve made a name for ourselves across the whole industry — and our biggest rival has been knocked flat. We’ll definitely make money on the next project. And this project got our company’s qualifications, the team’s teamwork and the supply chain all running smoothly. I’m confident we’ll definitely make big money in the new year.”

Wu You smiled, a very faint smile, and said, “Old Zheng, I understand all that. But I’m someone who runs a real business, and intangible assets don’t show up on a statement. What the statement shows is that this project didn’t make money. The shareholders look at statements. But I’m confident too that we can make money in the new year.”

Old Zheng said, “Mr. Wu, you really should be confident. The whole team’s working on two more bids that are pretty much about to come through — a hardware night-vision device for the Seventh Academy, and a supplementary contract for a simulation system at the Sixth Academy. And there’s one more thing. Several of the key people on the technical team keep asking, and I made them a promise too. We agreed back then on two blocks of equity, one of ten percent and one of six percent, to be changed over once the project was done. I’d like us to try to get it done as soon as possible, so I can keep the team steady.”

Wu You said, “I know. Before you came this time, I talked with the other shareholders about getting it done for you. But when the year’s accounts were added up there was no profit, and the other shareholders aren’t happy. If you want me to transfer it right now, I can’t. We’ll have to wait for the next project and show a profit before I can speak up at the shareholders’ meeting.”

Old Zheng said, “It’s true this is a touchy moment to bring it up. Then, Mr. Wu, I have one more request, if you’ll forgive me. A lot of the team took pay cuts to come here. I’d like to apply for a project bonus to pay year-end bonuses, to keep morale steady. How much could you approve for that?”

Wu You said, “You decide the figure. Get the accounts straight. Once the whole project’s money is collected in the first quarter, or we’ve got new revenue and we can break even, all the profit part — you can share it out with the team.”
Old Zheng said nothing.
Wu You said, “Old Zheng, why don’t you call Ms. Cong, and I’ll take the two of you to dinner tonight?”
Old Zheng said, “Oh, Mr. Wu, the two of us have a dinner with a client in Shanghai tonight — the end-user unit for the night-vision product. That leader is pretty hard to get a meeting with.”
Wu You said, “Then you take care of the client. We’re all family here — we can get together anytime.”
Old Zheng said, “Right. Mr. Wu, I’ll be going, then.”

Wu You said, “Old Zheng, you’re technically solid and you work like hell. I trust you. But in business you have to do the math. Signing the agreement with Gaoda the way you did — it’s hard to stop outsiders from looking at it and thinking something’s off. From now on, be more careful about things like that, and the company can’t fail to make money. Charge ahead all you like. I’ll handle the shareholders.”
Old Zheng said, “Thank you for your support, Mr. Wu.”
Wu You was supposedly three or four years younger than Old Zheng, but the way he handled people was so seasoned it was as if he thought like a man ten years older.

When he came out of Wu You’s office, Old Zheng stood at the entrance to the office tower. The Shanghai winter wind was damp and cold and crept in at his collar. He lit a cigarette, took two drags and stubbed it out in the trash can by the door. Shasha was waving at him frantically from behind the coffee shop’s glass, and when he didn’t see her she came out to call him in: “Come on, into the coffee shop. Let’s have something to drink before we go.”
Shasha ordered two more Americanos and set one across from her. Old Zheng sat down opposite her, picked up the coffee, drank and said, “It didn’t go well.”
Cong Shasha said, “How much will the year-end bonus be?”
Old Zheng said, “As good as nothing. How are those other two bids of ours coming along? How sure are we?”

Cong Shasha said, “I’ve had drinks with the leaders several times now. I’ve worked out who’s who. Technically we’re definitely fine — there aren’t many in the whole industry better than us. It’s just the person in charge of technology on the inside, that Dr. Xiao — she’s a bit odd, hard to read. Brother Yong, I think you’ll have to go work on her yourself. The simulation system development — Old Wu at the Sixth Academy introduced us to that one. That project’s bigger, but it’s still early — it’s only just been approved. That one’s going to take some grinding.”
Old Zheng listened and said nothing. Shasha asked, “No chance of a year-end bonus, then?”

Old Zheng said, “Don’t worry. Even if no one else gets one, you will.” Old Zheng knew perfectly well he still had two gold bars in his safe, and the price of gold had gone up a good deal in the past half year.
Cong Shasha said, “Brother Yong, I can see you’re not happy. It didn’t go well, did it?”

Old Zheng said, “Wu You keeps his books in more detail than I do. 1.8 million in rent, more than half a million in layoff costs, all the costs for the pile of people he put in — he counted it all, and for the whole year there’s basically no profit. Sigh.”

Cong Shasha picked up her coffee, took a sip, looked at Old Zheng and said, “Brother Yong, not losing money is pretty good already. We’ve kept all these people fed. From here on we’ll definitely make big money.”

Old Zheng said, “Still — I was too driven by feeling in that negotiation with Gaoda. All I was thinking about back then was killing off Yuanwang. Now people suspect I might have taken kickbacks through procurement.”
Cong Shasha said, “Brother Yong, I know you’re not that kind of person.”
Old Zheng said nothing. Shasha put down her cup and asked again, “So did you talk to Mr. Wu about your equity?”
Old Zheng said, “I did.”
Cong Shasha said, “And?”
Old Zheng said, “No chance.”

Cong Shasha said, “How can he be like that? You made the project a success! You’ve won the Sixth Academy’s name for us — that’s what makes the next projects easier to negotiate. Can’t he do that math?”
Old Zheng said, “He can do it. He just doesn’t want to transfer it to me now. Come on, I’ll take you for a big dinner.”

Cong Shasha said okay, got up and followed close behind Old Zheng on the way out. She had seen the two bosses meet with her own eyes today — in that grand river-view office, Wu You’s ease as the host, Old Zheng’s wariness. Suddenly it came clear to her: in that little patch of ground in Xi’an everyone took Old Zheng for the boss of the company, but in front of Wu You he was only a general who could fight battles, not a king who’d get a share of the realm. When the project succeeded, that was the company’s; making the equity official was the shareholders’ business. Wu You blocked him with the financial accounts, and Old Zheng had no fight in him at all.

While they waited for the car, Shasha said, “Brother Yong, don’t rush. The equity thing — you can’t rush it. Get the next project done first. Then if he still won’t transfer it, you’ll have cards in your hand.”
Old Zheng said, “I know.”

Cong Shasha said, “The night-vision hardware project — as long as you win over Dr. Xiao, it’s a sure thing. The simulation system one, I’m keeping an eye on too. If we land both projects, we’ll be fine for sure.”
The car arrived. Old Zheng said, “Why can’t you stop talking about work, girl? Are we going or not? Your big brother’s taking you to dinner.”
Cong Shasha reached out and gave his back a rub and said, “Let’s go — and once we’ve eaten, straight back to the hotel.”
Old Zheng said, “You’re planning on two meals in a row?”
Cong Shasha said, “Is that not allowed?”
Old Zheng glanced at her and said, smiling all over his face, “How could it not be allowed?”
The hotel room wasn’t big: one big bed, one window, and outside the window the night view of Huaihai Road, the lights on, the traffic crawling slowly past.

The two of them came in. Cong Shasha put down her bag, took off her coat and hung it in the wardrobe. Old Zheng sat on the edge of the bed and took off his shoes. Cong Shasha came over, sat down beside him without a word and leaned on his shoulder. Old Zheng reached out and drew her in.

What came after, neither of them rushed. She kissed him first, very lightly, as if testing. He kissed her back, his hand moving up from her waist. Her breathing slowly grew heavier; her hands rested on the back of his neck, fingertips slipping into his hair.

Their clothes came off one by one and were draped over the back of the chair. Only the bedside lamp was on, its light very dim, falling on the covers. Her body pressed against him, warm. His hand moved over her back, slowly, stroke by stroke.
Shasha’s body grew hot, rippling like a wave.
When it was over, the two of them lay side by side, catching their breath for a while. The room was very quiet, with only the hum of the air-conditioning vent.
After a while, Cong Shasha rolled over with her back to him, pulled his hand over and laid it on her waist, and gradually her breathing evened out and she fell fast asleep.
Just then, Old Zheng’s phone lit up. He reached for it and looked. It was a WeChat from Xiaoya: “Big brother, I’m thinking of coming to Xi’an for some fun next month. Will you show me around?”
He looked at the message for a few seconds.
He replied: “Come on, then. I’ll show you around.”
Then he went on lying there, looking at the ceiling. Outside, the lights of Huaihai Road were still on, their glow leaking through the gap in the curtains and falling on the carpet.
